name: Omar Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What fills an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the electricity company's industrial feeder repair crew, tracing faults between yards where several firms share access roads. I'm 43 with a two-year technical diploma, and I like finding the one failed connector behind a long outage. What wears me out is waiting at a gate while nobody can confirm which firm's equipment is live.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a pharmacist, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My lineworker pay is above the usual rate, we have about ten months of expenses saved and there are plenty of other utility crews nearby. I use AI every day to sort fault reports, but I have the crew check the meter before touching a feeder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the AI boom was louder than the actual change, but my daily fault search still earns its place. The industrial feeder still needs workers who can isolate a damaged section and replace the hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our household is sound for now: my lineworker pay is good, my partner's pharmacy shifts are steady and we have about ten months of expenses saved. I would not turn a small software gain into a risky career move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the industrial feeder repairs and use the AI fault search I already run at the start of each shift. For the next four jobs I'll check its suggested fault location against the meter readings before our truck moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with room to keep experimenting. I like a tool that saves one wasted drive, even if it never becomes a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where has the search sent your crew wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once sent us to the far end of a feeder because two sites had similar names. I corrected the label from the meter readings before the truck left our yard. My AI fault search once chose the wrong industrial feeder; the meter reading kept our truck at the right yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on more AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings account stays for household emergencies, not an AI purchase. My partner and I would keep the normal mortgage payment and take the children to their weekend games.

say: **Fault search** saves some drives, but workers still isolate and repair industrial feeders.
**Meter readings** must settle the fault location before the truck moves.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** and two steady wages leave us comfortable with mild change.
A small **software gain** is no reason to abandon a skilled lineworker role.
do: **Keep** leading industrial feeder repairs and daily fault searches.
**Compare** four suggested fault locations with meter readings before dispatch.
feel: **Calm** about income and interested in modest tool improvements.
S0.quote: My AI fault search once chose the wrong industrial feeder; the meter reading kept our truck at the right yard.
fieldNote: He already uses **AI daily** but checks its output against physical electrical readings.
Two wages and **ten months saved** support his calm without any new investment.

steps.text: Keep industrial feeder repair rota and daily fault search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI will buy fittings and flag faults earlier, while robots will take longer to repair lines in a crowded industrial yard. The company should let crew leads test the new fault system against real breakdowns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could benefit if the system removes wrong trips, but fewer dispatchers might mean my crew gets orders without a second check. My job seems secure; the worry is a hurried repair beside equipment that other firms still have running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll run the approved AI fault checker on ten completed feeder incidents and compare its suggestions with the actual repair sheets. If it finds the right faults, I'll ask for a paid pilot on current jobs and teach the crew to mark bad matches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about rushed handoffs, but not about my wage. I enjoy testing a tool when the crew can reject it on evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a wrong feeder label?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd block the order, call the site operator and confirm which feeder is live before anyone opens a cabinet. Two firms can label one industrial gate differently; the AI fault checker does not get the last word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you include in the pilot report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would report every false match as well as the time saved. If the manager sees only the faster cases, we will be told to leave the yard before checking the live status.

say: **AI fault checks** should be tested against real feeder repairs before crews rely on them.
**Field robots** will reach crowded industrial yards later than software reaches buying and dispatch.
think: My **repair wage** looks secure, and the new tool might reduce wasted trips.
Fewer **dispatch checks** could leave a hurried crew beside live equipment.
do: **Test** the approved checker on ten completed feeder incidents.
**Pilot** the checker on current jobs if the historical test identifies faults reliably.
feel: **Uneasy** about handoffs and safety, with job income still secure.
S1.quote: Two firms can label one industrial gate differently; the AI fault checker does not get the last word.
fieldNote: His trial has a **ten-case test** and tracks false matches, not just saved minutes.
He wants a **paid current-job pilot** rather than simply requesting a product brochure.

steps.text: Test approved AI checker on ten completed feeder incidents
Pilot approved checker on current jobs if historical test succeeds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could change fault diagnosis and dispatch quickly, while capable line robots around 2031 could take routine feeder repairs. The company should give skilled workers actual paid roles in testing those machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can adapt and we have ten months saved, but losing my lineworker hours would still alter our mortgage plan. My partner's pharmacy work might change in its paperwork too; I cannot assume either wage is untouched. Ten months of savings buys my family time; it does not make lost power-line hours free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask for the company's 2028 dispatch and 2031 field staffing plan and put my name forward for a paid robot repair pilot if a place opens. I'll ask two nearby utilities about lead crew vacancies, so I know what the market is before any shift cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible hour loss, though I have choices and enough cash to make them carefully. I do not expect a dismissal notice in my pocket tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children I am checking where the work might move, not that we are losing the house. The ten-month reserve is there if a transition takes time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a robot pilot actual work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the pilot only at my normal wage with access to its safety controls. A demonstration behind a barrier would not teach me how to stop a machine beside a live feeder.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches fault diagnosis before field robots arrive around 2031.
Skilled workers need **paid pilot roles** and a published crew plan.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** lets me search carefully, but lost line hours would still affect the mortgage.
My partner's **pharmacy paperwork** may change even while patient-facing shifts continue.
do: **Ask** management for 2028 dispatch and 2031 field staffing plans.
**Join** a paid robot repair pilot if offered with normal wages and safety controls.
**Check** nearby utilities for actual lead crew vacancies before any cut.
feel: **Anxious** about possible crew-hour loss, with local options and a cash buffer.
S2.quote: Ten months of savings buys my family time; it does not make lost power-line hours free.
fieldNote: He has **financial runway** and several utility employers, yet names realistic hour risk.
His robot pilot condition is **normal wages** and real controls, not passive observation.
He checks vacancies before a cut but makes no claim of an **offer**.

steps.text: Ask company for 2028 dispatch and 2031 crew staffing plans
Join paid repair robot pilot if normal wage and controls offered
Check nearby utilities for open lead line crew posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test field robots on an actual feeder fault before they reach crews around 2034. The 2031 thinking system could improve diagnosis first, which gives us a chance to find its blind spots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid repair-robot supervisor post could fit me, if the company creates one. I also know how a pilot can remove routine calls and leave fewer training jobs for the younger crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll use the approved AI diagnosis tool on six real incidents this year and record where its proposed isolation differs from the meter readings. If the company then offers a paid robot controls course with supervised field practice, I'll enrol while retaining my lead crew wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the apprentices and crew mix, though I can test the tools early. I do not need a guaranteed new title to start gathering evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fault log actually record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd log the feeder name, the wrong isolation suggestion and the reading that corrected it. The supervisor needs to see exactly which error could send a crew to the wrong cabinet. A wrong AI isolation can send my power-line crew to the wrong live cabinet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the course include before you enrol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the course on paid time, followed by supervised work at a real yard. If it is only online lessons with no field practice, I will keep the normal repair roster.

say: **Six real incidents** can reveal where thinking AI misreads an industrial feeder.
A **paid controls course** should include supervised field work before 2034 robots arrive.
think: A robot supervisor **vacancy** may suit me, but no such paid post is guaranteed.
Reduced **routine calls** could weaken apprentice practice even if I retain work.
do: **Test** approved AI diagnosis on six incidents and record wrong isolations.
**Enrol** in a paid robot controls course if supervised field practice is offered.
feel: **Uneasy** about future crew mix, yet interested in early tests.
S3.quote: A wrong AI isolation can send my power-line crew to the wrong live cabinet.
fieldNote: His trial uses **real incidents** and meter readings, a meaningful test for thinking AI.
The course is a **conditional enrolment** with paid time and supervised field practice.

steps.text: Test approved AI diagnosis on six incidents and record wrong isolations
Enrol in paid robot controls course if supervised field practice offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to teach the next crew both line isolation and machine controls. Thinking AI in 2036 changes diagnosis first, and capable field robots around 2039 change repairs, so the company should show the whole path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By the 2039 robot stage, at 56 I might run a paid field testing team or stay on repairs if the work is there. With ten months saved and good nearby job options, I can wait for an actual offer instead of buying a future title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my line safety tickets current and teach apprentices how we confirm a feeder before opening it. Each year I'll check paid field-testing vacancies and compare their wages with my lead crew pay before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to see the long view, with a little worry about apprentices losing basic repairs. I could use the decade to teach carefully rather than scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprentice do before trusting diagnosis AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the apprentice identify the correct feeder from the cabinet label and meter reading, then compare the AI's diagnosis. The machine may be useful, but the worker must know how to catch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take a field-testing post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A field-testing position needs a real roster, authority to stop unsafe work and pay near my current wage. I would not leave a lead lineworker job for a title alone. A field-testing title without a roster and stop-work authority would not replace my lineworker wage.

say: **Apprentices** need line isolation skills alongside new machine controls before 2039.
**2036 thinking AI** changes diagnosis before robots change physical repair work.
think: By **2039**, at 56, paid field testing could suit me if a real post opens.
Our **ten-month reserve** and local utility jobs let me wait for sound terms.
do: **Renew** line safety tickets and keep teaching feeder isolation.
**Check** paid field-testing vacancies yearly for wages and stop-work authority.
feel: **Calm** about long-term choices, with concern for apprentice repair practice.
S4.quote: A field-testing title without a roster and stop-work authority would not replace my lineworker wage.
fieldNote: He links later roles to **written duties**, wages and safety authority.
His long runway protects **family choice** while keeping real apprentice repair skills visible in the workplace.

steps.text: Renew line safety tickets and teach feeder isolation
Check paid field-testing vacancies for wages and stop-work authority yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because thinking AI would change diagnosis quickly and capable field robots around 2031 could cut repair hours. A clear crew forecast and a paid pilot with actual safety controls would help me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can stop a repair robot when two industrial firms label one gate differently. I would teach that rule before any new tool goes live. My power-line crew must be able to halt a robot at the feeder, not wait for a distant screen to catch up.

headlineQuote: My power-line crew must be able to halt a robot at the feeder, not wait for a distant screen to catch up.
portrait: **Omar**, 43, leads industrial feeder repairs and uses a two-year technical diploma to trace stubborn faults.
He uses **AI daily** for fault reports but checks its conclusions against electrical readings.
His **higher pay**, pharmacist partner, ten-month savings and nearby utilities give the family options.
He would seek **paid robot controls** and real field authority before leaving his lead crew role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves limited time before capable field robots around 2031 may reduce paid repair hours.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **crew forecast** and paid pilot with real safety controls would help him plan.
